title: Only 180 days for plunder trials
primary_topics: SC March 18, 2014 resolution: terminate regular trial within 180 days, or trial by judicial affidavits within 60 days, 'reckoned from the date trial begins, minus the excluded delays or postponements specified in Rule 119 of the Rules of Court and the Speedy Trial Act of 1998'

Pre-trial timeline breaches: case must first be raffled within 3 days of information filing; pork plunder cases actually raffled to First/Third/Fifth SBN Divisions one week after filing (4 days beyond 3-day limit)
10-day arraignment limit also breached -- arraignment took place much later because three divisions had to first determine probable cause and issue warrants

10-day pretrial conference limit also breached -- pretrial 6-element enumeration (plea bargaining + stipulation of facts + marking of evidence + waiver of admissibility objections + lawful-defense modification + fair-expeditious-trial promotion)

Pre-trial proceedings menu: (1) motion for bail (burden on prosecution to prove evidence-of-guilt-strong; speed-up via June 29 column / A408); (2) motion to suspend detained senators under Anti-Plunder Law (90-days-vs-trial-duration open question); (3) motions for reconsideration, bills of particulars, medical treatment, hospital arrest, detention site, postponement, quashing

Rule 119 + Speedy Trial Act excluded delays enumeration: (a) physical/mental condition, other criminal charges, extraordinary remedies, pre-trial proceedings, inhibition orders, change of venue, prejudicial questions, proceedings under advisement; (b) absent/unavailable essential witnesses; (c) mental incompetence/physical inability to stand trial; (d) refiling of dismissed charge; (e) co-accused arrest joining; (f) trial-court 'outweigh best interest' balancing
Fourth concern: SBN orders on these items would surely be elevated to SC; TROs could indefinitely delay trial
'I think the plunder proceedings will definitely exceed the 180- and 60-day limits' candid forecast

Estrada plunder trial precedent: took 6+ years in one SBN Special Division with only 3 accused, fewer witnesses, less evidence; final decision in 5 years (10x 180-day limit) 'would be phenomenal'; speedy-trial-failure dismissal sanction

stances.claim: How long will the trial of the pork barrel plunder cases last? The SC directed trial courts 'to terminate the regular trial within 180 days, or the trial by judicial affidavits within 60 days, reckoned from the date trial begins, minus the excluded delays or postponements specified in Rule 119 of the Rules of Court and the Speedy Trial Act of 1998'; these limits apply to all criminal cases whenever the accused are detained pending trial (per SC resolution dated March 18, 2014); 'regular trial' refers to the question-and-answer method; 'trial by judicial affidavits' is via submission of affidavits

stances.claim: First -- time limits 'reckoned from the date trial begins,' but before trial can begin the case must first be raffled, which the edict says should be held 'within three days from the filing of the information'; the pork plunder cases were actually raffled to the First, Third and Fifth Divisions of the SBN one week after filing -- four days beyond the 3-day limit; under the resolution, the 'trial court shall arraign the accused within 10 days from the date of the raffle,' but this was also breached because the three divisions had to first determine probable cause and issue arrest warrants; the resolution also says the 'court shall hold the pre-trial conference within 10 days if the accused is under preventive detention,' again not followed

Pretrial is conducted by the judge and the parties to consider: (a) plea bargaining; (b) stipulation of facts; (c) marking for identification of evidence; (d) waiver of objections to admissibility; (e) modification of the order of trial if the accused admits the charge but interposes a lawful defense (like self-defense); and (f) other matters that promote a fair and expeditious trial -- given alone the 'truckloads' of documents to be marked as exhibits in the three SBN divisions, the pretrial could be quite lengthy

Pre-trial proceedings include: (1) motion for bail -- detained accused (including the three senators) filed separate motions; the burden is on the prosecution to show 'evidence of guilt is strong'; if it fails, the accused are entitled to bail; how to speed up bail hearings was discussed in CJ's June 29 column (A408 'Supreme Court speeds up bail hearings'); (2) motion to suspend the detained senators under the Anti-Plunder Law -- whether Congress will recognize such suspension and for how long (90 days only or trial duration) are open questions; (3) motions for reconsideration, bills of particulars, medical treatment, hospital arrest, better detention site, postponement, to quash, etc.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the procedural-doctrinal companion column to his bail-hearings piece two weeks earlier (A408 June 29). How long will the trial of the pork barrel plunder cases last? Answer: the SC directed trial courts 'to terminate the regular trial within 180 days, or the trial by judicial affidavits within 60 days, reckoned from the date trial begins, minus the excluded delays or postponements specified in Rule 119 of the Rules of Court and the Speedy Trial Act of 1998.' Analysis: these 180- and 60-day limits apply to all criminal cases whenever the accused is/are detained pending trial, per a resolution of the SC dated March 18, 2014. 'Regular trial' refers to the question-and-answer method of examining witnesses while 'trial by judicial affidavits' is conducted via the submission of affidavits. Let us analyze the high court's order. First, the time limits shall be 'reckoned from the date trial begins.' However, before trial can begin, the case must first be raffled, which the edict says should be held 'within three days from the filing of the information' -- the pork plunder cases were actually raffled to the First, Third and Fifth Divisions of the Sandiganbayan one week after they were filed, four days beyond the 3-day limit. Also, under the resolution, 'the trial court shall arraign the accused within 10 days from the date of the raffle' -- again, this limit was breached: the arraignment took place much later because the three divisions had to determine first the existence of probable cause and to issue the warrants of arrest. The resolution further says, 'The [trial] court shall hold the pre-trial conference within 10 days if the accused is under preventive detention' -- again, this limit was not followed. Pretrial is conducted by the judge and the parties 'to consider the following: (a) plea bargaining; (b) stipulation of facts; (c) marking for identification of evidence of the parties; (d) waiver of objections to admissibility of evidence; (e) modification of the order of trial if the accused admits the charge but interposes a lawful defense (like self-defense); and (f) such other matters as will promote a fair and expeditious trial' -- given alone the 'truckloads' of documents to be marked as exhibits in the three SBN divisions, the pretrial could be quite lengthy. (1) Motion for bail: the detained accused, including the three senators, filed separate motions for bail; the burden of proof is on the prosecution to show that the 'evidence of guilt is strong'; if the prosecution fails, the accused are entitled to be released on bail; how to speed up the bail hearings under the same March 18 resolution was discussed in CJ's June 29 column (A408). (2) Motion to suspend the detained senators as provided under the Anti-Plunder Law -- whether Congress will recognize such suspension and for how long (90 days only or duration of trial) are open questions. (3) Motions for reconsideration, bills of particulars, medical treatment, hospital arrest, better detention site, postponement, to quash the information, etc. Third, apart from these, the resolution excludes the 'delays specified in Rule 119 of the Rules of Court and the Speedy Trial Act': (a) any period of delay concerning the accused (physical/mental condition, other criminal charges in other SBN divisions, extraordinary remedies against interlocutory orders, pre-trial proceedings, orders of inhibition and change of venue, prejudicial question, proceedings under advisement); (b) absence or unavailability of essential witnesses; (c) mental incompetence or physical inability of the accused to stand trial; (d) refiling of a previously dismissed charge; (e) when a co-accused who had been at large is arrested and joined in the case; (f) in general, delays which the trial court believes 'outweigh the best interest of the public and the accused in a speedy trial.' If you are confused and beguiled by these excluded delays, don't be surprised if creative lawyers invent more perplexities to further befuddle you. Fourth: the SBN orders resolving the above items would surely be elevated to the SC; if the Court issues temporary restraining orders, the trial could be indefinitely delayed. At bottom, considering the complicated nature of plunder, the very many accused, the numerous witnesses, the 'truckloads' of documentary evidence, the many exceptions to the March 18 resolution, the many other incidents prior trial, and the diverse rulings on some of these incidents by the three SBN divisions, CJ thinks the plunder proceedings will definitely exceed the 180- and 60-day limits. In fact, a final decision by any of the three divisions in five years (that's 10 times the 180-day limit) 'would be phenomenal,' given that the plunder trial of Joseph Estrada in one SBN Special Division took over six years, yet there were only three accused, fewer witnesses and less amount of evidence. Hastening the pork plunder cases is indeed a major challenge. Unjustified delay carries a heavy sanction because, to quote the resolution, 'the cases against the detained accused may be dismissed on ground of denial of the right to speedy trial in the event of failure to observe the above time limits.'
